source.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
source.authors: Yunzhi Yao; Ning-Yu Zhang; Ze-Kun Xi; Meng-Ru Wang; Ziwen Xu; Shu-Min Deng; Hua-Jun Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study identifies attention heads in in-context-learning circuits as induction-like and tests their contribution by ablating them, using circuit analysis rather than the original study’s training-dynamics measurements.
record.gate_note: The in-context-learning analysis describes heads attending to demonstrations and calls them induction heads; Table 2 reports performance before and after ablating those heads or random heads. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. The study does not measure training-time formation, token-index loss changes, or the loss curve.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the induction-head label to describe heads that join a GPT-2 knowledge circuit when a one-shot demonstration is added, but it does not test any version. It gives no induction or prefix-matching score and no previous-token composition. It does not measure training dynamics or loss against token index. The heads are called induction heads only from qualitative attention patterns in one example (Fig. 5b). Table 2 shows that ablating these demonstration-attending heads lowers task performance more than ablating a random head. That is a finding about circuit components for knowledge in-context learning, not a measured rate or strength of induction behaviour. The model and metric for Table 2 are also unstated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report that new attention heads attending to the demonstration appear in the knowledge circuit during in-context learning. They describe these heads, qualitatively, as working like induction heads. Ablating them drops the prediction probability significantly more than ablating random heads. The authors link this to function vectors (Todd et al.), not just to induction heads.
record.recipe_differences: Uses knowledge-circuit discovery and head ablation in selected in-context-learning cases; it does not reproduce the original training-time induction-head and loss-curve analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ablation effects vary by knowledge/task condition; random-head ablation also lowers performance for some conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: In a knowledge-recall setting (likely GPT2-Medium), adding a one-shot demonstration brings new heads into the circuit that attend to the demonstration. Ablating them lowers task scores far more than ablating a random head, e.g. adj_comparative 62.24→32.55 vs 58.18, and word_sentiment 89.02→55.50 vs 88.61.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heads attending to demonstrations, described qualitatively as induction-like, are causally important for demonstration-based knowledge recall in pretrained GPT-2.

record.problems: The in-context-learning evidence is limited to five listed task conditions. The model used for Table 2 is not stated there, the performance metric is not further specified in the table, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The analysis does not test the proposed previous-token-head composition or training-time dynamics.

untested.parts: All of it. The models are not small attention-only transformers, there is no previous-token head or composition analysis, and the [A][B]…[A]→[B] behaviour is not measured.
All of it; there is no training-time analysis.
All of it. Loss is not measured against token index, and the heads are not verified as induction heads. Few-shot knowledge accuracy is not the version's in-context learning measure.
All of it. Induction heads are not identified systematically across GPT2-Medium, GPT2-Large and TinyLLaMA.
All of it. The study does not separate induction heads from other mechanisms (e.g. function-vector heads) in few-shot learning; it only mentions function vectors.

record.verdict_notes: This is a knowledge-circuits paper (GPT-2 Medium/Large, TinyLLaMA); in-context learning is a short sub-analysis in Section 6. The induction label comes from one illustrative attention pattern, with no induction score. The model and metric for Table 2 are not stated, and no uncertainty is reported. The record's V1 'supports' label is dropped, because V1 concerns the previous-token composition mechanism in small attention-only models, which the study does not examine.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines induction-like attention heads and their contribution in selected in-context-learning tasks, but does not test composition with an earlier previous-token head or establish the full mechanism in small attention-only transformers.
